top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Grossman, citation confined to the political economy of trade protection) has the cleanest attribution on the slate: a long, tightly coupled two-person programme with joint papers and a book, so nobody at the same level is excluded. Protection-for-sale turned trade protection from an exogenous policy variable into the equilibrium of lobbying and government objectives. It produced sharp, falsifiable cross-sector predictions and about three decades of theory, testing and policy analysis, so maturity is not in doubt. The empirical record is mixed and specification-sensitive, so the citation should claim a framework and research programme, not confirmed parameters. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is second. Its design-based evidence is strong and the three-name set is now stable, but the task-framework antecedents are uncredited and the long-run size and persistence of the China-shock effects and the shift-share identification are still being revised. P003 (Melitz, Helpman) is third. Its empirical confrontation is dense, but the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum attribution gap cannot be closed within the credited set and the contribution rests heavily on one 2003 paper. I rank an award above no award because P001 and P002 are both substantive and defensible. This judgement rests on the written round-2 record and general knowledge, not independent verification, and the number of supporters is not treated as merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my listed co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen, Robinson, Martinsson, Thomann) are not credited on P001, P002 or P003. For disclosure only: adjunct professor at Chicago Booth, Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, and a long overlap with several committee colleagues. These are not candidate-specific conflicts and are disclosed without adjudication.
